    1                                      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

    2          On June 17, 2026, Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “Company”) filed

    3          an Application with the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“Commission”) requesting

    4          the Commission approve an Extra Large Power and Light Tariff, (“XLPL”), and the Terms

    5          and Conditions of Service for Extra Large Load Customers, (“T&CXLLC”), and a

    6          regulatory asset to track costs associated with the implementation of portfolio optimization

    7          modeling software.



    8          The Commission’s Public Utility Division (“PUD”) reviewed the Application, direct

    9          testimony filed by Company witnesses, and prior Commission Orders. PUD issued data

   10          requests and reviewed the responses provided by OG&E as well as the responses to data

   11          requests issued by other parties in the case.



   12          After review, PUD recommends the Commission find that OG&E’s proposed XLPL Tariff

   13          and the T&CXLLC contain reasonable customer protections and satisfy the requirements

   14          enumerated in 17 O.S. Section 903 including credit and collateral requirements, minimum

   15          billing provisions, and a minimum contract term.



   16          PUD does not, however, ask the Commission to find that the filing as made discharges the

   17          cost-causation standard of 17 O.S. Section 902 or the requirement in Section 903 that the

   18          terms, conditions, and tariffs include “any other measures necessary” to ensure that large

   19          load customers reimburse the electric supplier for all costs fairly allocated to them. The

   20          Application supplies the structural protections the statute enumerates but does not supply

    2          other than full bundled generation service from OG&E, and asks for a regulatory asset for

    1                                               PURPOSE

    2    Q:    What is the purpose of your testimony regarding OG&E’s application in this Case?

    3    A:    The purpose of my Responsive Testimony is to present PUD’s recommendations to the

    4          Commission regarding OG&E’s proposed:

    5          1) XLPL Tariff;

    6          2) T&CXLLC; and

    7          3) Regulatory Asset associated with Portfolio Optimization Software.



    8                                     PUD’S REVIEW PROCESS

    9    Q:    Please explain PUD’s review process in this Case.

   10    A:    PUD reviewed the Application and the Company’s direct testimony. PUD also reviewed

   11          data requests issued to OG&E as well as those issued by intervenors, and the associated

   12          responses. Additionally, PUD reviewed prior Commission orders and testimony, including

   13          the record and the Joint Stipulation and Settlement Agreement in Case No. PUD 2025-

   14          000075, and the pending application in Case No. PUD2026-000031.



   15                               PROPOSED LARGE LOAD TARIFF

   16    Q:    Was OG&E required to make this filing?

   17    A:    Yes. Commission Order No. 753440 in Case No. PUD2025-000038 ordered OG&E to

   18          seek approval of a new large load tariff by July 1, 2026, through a docketed proceeding

   19          with the draft tariff, along with explanations and support for the tariff.

    1    Q:       Does this filing meet the requirements of Commission Order No. 753440?

    2    A:       Yes, as to the obligation to file. Order No. 753440 required OG&E to submit a draft tariff

    3             with supporting explanation by July 1, 2026, and to file the portfolio optimization cost-

    4             benefit study at the same time. OG&E did both. Whether the content of the filing should

    5             be approved as filed is a separate question, addressed in the balance of my testimony.



    6    Q:       Did House Bill 2992 (“HB 2992”) known as the Data Center Customer Ratepayer

    7             Protection Act of 2026 affect the timing of this Case?

    8    A:       Yes. HB 2992, codified as 17 O.S. Section 900 et seq., became effective on July 1, 2026,

    9             and was enacted to “ensure that residential, commercial and industrial customers are

   10             protected from paying unjust rates resulting directly from electric service to large load

   11             customers,” 1 and that “all rates are fair, just and reasonable, and costs and revenues are
                                if




   12             assigned and allocated among customers in accordance with cost causation principles.” 2



   13             To accomplish these goals, the new law addressing electric suppliers:

   14                       […] shall establish and maintain separate terms and conditions of service
   15                       applicable to any large load customer and shall create and maintain separate
   16                       tariffs applicable to such large load customers. These terms, conditions, and
   17                       tariffs shall include credit requirements and any other measures necessary
   18                       to ensure that such customers reimburse the electric supplier for all costs
   19                       fairly allocated to them […], including costs incurred to directly serve the
   20                       customer that may remain unrecovered if the customer departs the system
   21                       or materially reduces load. 3

         Q:         Does this filing comply with the requirements of HB 2992?

    1    A:         As my following testimony will show, the filing satisfies the requirements 17 O.S. Section

    2               903 enumerates, separate terms and conditions, a separate tariff, credit and collateral

    3               requirements, minimum billing provisions, and minimum contract term. It does not yet

    4               satisfy the balance of Section 903, which requires “any other measures necessary” to ensure

    5               reimbursement of all costs fairly allocated to large load customers, or the cost-causation

    6               standard of Section 902, because the filing does not prescribe how cost causation is to be

    7               measured. The Customer Impact Review attached as Exhibit DS-3 supplies that measure.



    8    Q:         Please provide an overview of the XLPL tariff proposed by OG&E.

    9    A:         The XLPL Tariff is a new retail electric service rate schedule being proposed by the

   10               Company to serve customers whose electric demands meet the requirements outlined in

   11               HB 2992. The tariff will be applicable to any customer meeting the definition of an XLPL

   12               customer as identified in the T&CXLLC, and service under the tariff requires a Preliminary

   13               Agreement (“PA”) and an Electric Service Agreement (“ESA”) as described in the

   14               T&CXLLC. 4



   15    Q:         How does the Company believe this tariff will benefit OG&E’s existing customer

   16               classes?

   17    A:         OG&E states that this tariff will benefit the Company’s existing customer classes by paying

   18               their allocated portion of all existing shared system costs. These large load customers will

   19               increase system usage and will help pay the existing costs of the entire system and will

    4    Q:         Does PUD agree with the Company’s belief?

    5    A:         With everything being equal, PUD would agree with the Company. However, going

    6               forward, the investment needed to serve these large load customers has the potential for

    7               adverse impacts on residential customers. The costs of energy and capacity going forward

    8               will likely be more expensive than the current supply serving no large load customers.

    9               Therefore, in the future, as new generation, capacity and energy costs are brought on board,

   10               the cost of that new generation should be allocated to the XLPL class to the extent it is

   11               caused by XLPL load. PUD opposes folding new, higher-cost supply into an average

   12               embedded cost allocated across all classes on a load-ratio share, so that residential

   13               customers pay a blended price that is higher than it would have been because extra-large

   14               load was added to the system. Allocation of these new generation costs should be borne

   15               by the new large load customers.

         Q:         Does the weaker collateral requirement concern PUD?

    1    Q:         What threshold or criteria would require a customer to take service under the

    2               proposed XLPL tariff?

    3    A:         A customer qualifies for the XLPL tariff if it meets the definition of any one of three

    4               customer types: 9

    5               •   Customer Type 1 is any customer beginning service after July 1, 2026, and is expected

    6                   to have an annual peak demand of 75 megawatts (“MW”) or more.

    7               •   Customer Type 2 is any customer taking service before July 1, 2026, whose future

    8                   billing demand is expected to either increase by 75 MW or more above its billing

    9                   demand prior to July 1, 2026, or to increase to a total demand of 125 MW or more.

   10               •   Customer Type 3 is an existing customer taking service before July 1, 2026, who may

   11                   not be adding load, but whose service conditions change in such a manner that OG&E

   12                   would be required to add generating capacity to meet a higher increase in demand for

   13                   that existing customer.



   14    Q:         Why did OG&E create three different types of customers?

   15    A:         The Company created three different types of customers to ensure that any customer

   16               (existing or new) that would result in OG&E having a new service obligation of 75 MW

   17               or more should be subject to the customer protections contained within the XLPL tariff and

    7    Q:     What circumstances could lead to an existing customer becoming a Type 3 customer?

    1    Q:        Does PUD have a concern with an open-ended Type 3 definition?

    2    A:        Yes. Types 1 and 2 are triggered by something the customer does, it takes new service, or

    3              it adds load. Type 3 is triggered by a change in “service conditions” that OG&E determines

    4              would require it to add capacity. Two of the three circumstances identified by OG&E are

    5              actions of SPP, not of the customer. An existing commercial customer or industrial

    6              customer could therefore be moved onto a fifteen-year tariff with a sixty-month collateral

    7              requirement, minimum bill, and an exit fee because SPP changed the reserve margin.

    8              Given this, PUD recommends that before OG&E classifies an existing customer as a Type

    9              3 customer, it provide written notice to the customer and to the Director of PUD identifying

   10              the change in service conditions relied upon and the accredited capacity OG&E asserts

   11              must be added, and the customer shall then have thirty (30) days to contest the classification

    1   Q:         Please provide a description of Portfolio Optimization Software.

    2   A:         Portfolio optimization is the process of evaluating many possible combinations of

    3              resources and selecting the mix that best meets defined objectives while respecting

    4              constraints. It starts by characterizing each option of a resource offered in terms of

    5              expected benefits, costs, risk, and performance under different future conditions. These

    6              options are then combined into portfolios and modeled through scenarios such as demand

    7              growth, fuel price variations, technology performance, or regulatory changes. The core

    8              idea of portfolio optimization tools is that many resource combinations can be evaluated

    9              quickly. Some resources may perform better than others in a particular scenario, but

   10              comparatively worse in a different scenario depending on how its components interact, not

   11              just on how each resource performs individually. 46

                                       CUSTOMER IMPACT REVIEW

                        Proposed Section 515 of the Terms and Conditions of Service

                                  for Extra Large Load Customers (Part V)

               515.01 Purpose.

               (a)     This Section establishes a uniform and objective methodology for determining

            whether, and to what extent, the Company’s provision of electric service to Extra Large Load

            Customers results in an adverse rate impact to other customer classes, and for preserving any

            amount so determined for Commission disposition in a general rate case.

               (b)     This Section is adopted pursuant to 17 O.S. §§ 902 and 903 as a measure necessary

            to ensure that Extra Large Load Customers reimburse the Company for all costs fairly allocated

            to them, and to give administrable content to the requirement that costs and revenues be

            assigned and allocated among customers in accordance with cost causation principles.

               (c)     This Section establishes a measurement and recording methodology only. It does

            not itself assign cost responsibility, modify any rate or charge, or determine the amount any

            customer or class shall pay.



               515.02 Application and Relationship to Section 506.

               (a)     Section 506 provides that any potential adverse rate impact to other customer rate

            classes because of the costs of providing service to the XLPL customer class will be reviewed

            and addressed by the Commission in each general rate case proceeding and each annual review

            proceeding of the Company’s Fuel Cost Adjustment rider.           This Section supplies the

            methodology by which that review is to be conducted. It does not limit, condition, or narrow

            the review Section 506 requires.

        “Contingent Resource” means a generation or capacity resource that the Company acquired,

               515.06 Methodology. Each Assessment shall compare:

               (a)     Base Case — actual operations and actual costs for the Assessment Year, including

            all Covered Customers taking service.

               (b)     What-If Case — the Base Case with the Covered Load removed, together with the

            generation capacity associated with serving that load and the costs of that capacity, determined

            under Sections 515.07 through 515.09.

               (c)     Both cases shall reflect all Company costs and revenues bearing on class cost

            responsibility, including net costs of generation resources, market costs and revenues, and

            transmission costs and revenues.

               (d)     Neither case shall remove load without also removing the costs incurred to serve

            that load, and neither case shall remove costs without also removing the corresponding load

            and billing units.

               (e)     The adverse impact to a customer class, if any, is the amount by which the net cost

            assigned to that class in the Base Case exceeds the net cost assigned to that class in the What-

            If Case.

               (f)     Where a Covered Customer self-supplies all or part of its capacity and energy

            requirements, the What-If Case shall remove only the portion of that customer’s Covered Load

            that is not attributable to its Self-Supplied Requirements, together with the capacity associated

            with serving that portion. Any standby, backup, or maintenance capacity the Company

            procures or retains on that customer’s account shall be treated as capacity associated with

            serving that customer’s Covered Load and shall be removed with it.

               515.07 Quantity of Capacity Removed. The capacity removed in the What-If Case

            equals the accredited MW required to serve the Covered Load in the Assessment Year,

            determined on the same accreditation basis the Southwest Power Pool applied for that year.

            No fixed or historical accreditation assumption shall be substituted for the accreditation

            determination applicable to the Assessment Year.



               515.08 Price Applied.

               (a)     Capacity removed under Section 515.07 shall be priced at the System Average Net

            Cost of Generation, expressed in $/kW-year.

               (b)     The SANCG equals the total net revenue requirement of all Applicable Generation

            Resources divided by the total accredited capacity, in kW, of those same resources.

               (c)     Net revenue requirement shall capture all fixed costs, fuel costs, and non-fuel

            variable costs, net of market revenues attributable to the resource.

               (d)     The average embedded cost of the total generation fleet shall not be used, and no

            component identified in subsection (c) shall be excluded.

               (e)     All Applicable Generation Resources are included without regard to whether a

            particular resource can be identified as having been added to serve Covered Load.



               515.09 Contingent Resources.

               (a)     The capacity and cost of each Contingent Resource shall be counted toward the cost

            of supplying the Covered Load of the customer whose agreement the resource was contingent

            upon and shall be removed in the What-If Case together with that load.

               515.14 Coordination with Other Class Protection Mechanisms.

               (a)     Amounts credited to a customer class for the Assessment Year through the

            resulting net adverse impact after netting under subsection (a).
